name: Middle Clarence Bandjalang
sweep_summary: midd1357 (Middle Clarence Bandjalang) is not in the catalog under this key; the same lect is coded in the catalog as band1339 'Bandjalang' (QS-HEDGED, carried-quote: Hayes 1980 pp.108-109/170 fn.2 and StressTyp2-carried Hammond 1986:193,195, all second-hand on Crowley 1978). The sweep's one item, Hammond 1986 NLLT 4 (DOI 10.1007/BF00133844), is relevant -- the Springer landing page (opened via web lookups) lists Crowley 1978 The Middle Clarence Dialects of Bandjalang in its references and StressTyp2 carries its Bandjalang sentences from pp.193/195 ('Main stress is generally initial, secondary stress on long vowels'; 'Words with main stress on the second vowel are only optional variants') -- but it is paywalled (Springer USD 39.95; Unpaywall closed; S2 closed; not on Hammond's Arizona/GitHub pages; CORE/BASE/IA Scholar blocked), so nothing in it was read first-hand: access = paywalled-doi, priority medium (it is a secondary analysis whose Bandjalang content is already carried verbatim by StressTyp2). The primary that would settle the coding, Crowley 1978 (AIAS, 492 pp; not among the sweep items), remains unreachable: archive.org middleclarencedi0000crow is lending/printdisabled only (metadata re-fetched sources; search-inside 'Item not available'; FTS 0 hits), HathiTrust is search-only and its API returned 403 from our machine, Google Books API quota exhausted, AIATSIS/Austlang behind Cloudflare, ANU Open Research has no Crowley item; priority HIGH for acquisition (library or IA borrow). Best first-hand statement actually read this sweep is Sharpe 1997 (PL C-136) p.372, already on file: stress is initial unless a non-initial syllable has a long vowel ('By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed'), corroborating the band1339 coding (initial, long-vowel-sensitive) without superseding it; Wikipedia's Stress section (fetched sources wikitext) attributes the same quantity-sensitive picture to Sharpe 2005:180 (LINCOM grammar, closed). Cunningham 1969:75 (Yugumbir, sister dialect, on file) gives 'first syllable... or the first long syllable if such is present'. All fetch receipts are in with.org/Wikipedia APIs and direct fetches.

new_statements.quote: Watson in particular uses some diacritics on certain vowels. An acute accent indicates stress usually when it falls on other than the first syllable. By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed.
new_statements.citation: Sharpe, Margaret C. 1997. Yugambeh-Bundjalung: what can be learnt from the dialect differences. In D. Tryon & M. Walsh (eds), Pacific Linguistics C-136: 363-392. Canberra: ANU (CC BY-SA; ANU Open Research handle 1885/253898).
new_statements.locator: p. 372, end of section 1 (the paragraph on Watson's diacritics), immediately before '2. Vowel shifts reliably noted in the different dialects'
new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by a linguist who worked on the whole Yugambeh-Bundjalung dialect chain, explicitly covering Crowley's (Middle Clarence) analysis: the default stressed syllable is the first, and where stress is perceived elsewhere than the first syllable the stressed syllable contains a long vowel -- i.e. initial stress, attracted to a long vowel (CVV-sensitive); it says nothing about which of several long vowels wins or about the disyllabic L-H variation reported by Hayes/Hammond. It is weaker than the (unreached) Crowley 1978 primary and than the StressTyp2-carried Hayes 1980 / Hammond 1986 rule, so it should be read as a corroborating first-hand statement, not as a new deciding source. Consistent with the sister-dialect primaries on file: Cunningham 1969:75 (Yugumbir) 'Stress occurs on the first syllable of the word, or on the first long syllable if such is present', and Hayes 1980:109 (carrying Crowley 1978 for Waalubal) 'the mirror image stress pattern [of Yapese] is reported for... the Waalubal dialect of Bandjalang', fn. 2 p.170 'Banjalang also ha[s] secondary stress, which falls on long vowels'.

"Words with main stress on the second vowel are only optional variants. (Hammond 1986:195)". Springer landing page (opened): reference list includes "Crowley, T.: 1978, The Middle Clarence Dialects of Bandjalang, Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies, Canberra"; conclusion preview: "ROB feet enable us to capture the fact that in certain positions (nonhead positions) under certain types of iteration or scanning (ROB types), heavy syllables are treated just like light syllables."
sources.locator: pp. 193 and 195 per StressTyp2 lect 878 (Waalubal) passages 1984-1985, carried; the paper itself was not opened
sources.note: A general metrical-theory article (obligatory-branching / 'ROB' feet) that uses Bandjalang (Waalubal, Middle Clarence; data second-hand from Crowley 1978, which is in its reference list per the Springer page) as one of its case languages. As carried by StressTyp2: main stress generally initial, secondary stress on long vowels, and words with main stress on the second vowel are only optional variants (i.e. the Hayes 1980 'mirror-image Yapese' rule -- stress the first syllable unless it is short and the second is long -- with variation).
